text: Listen to part of a talk in a biology class.
script: M: OK, so last time we looked at how owls hunt by sound. Today I want to talk about animals that don't just listen. They actually make the sound themselves. I'm talking about echolocation in bats.

M: Here's the basic idea. A bat produces very high-pitched calls, usually too high for us to hear. Those calls bounce off objects around it, and the bat listens to the echoes. From the time it takes an echo to return, the bat can tell how far away something is.

M: Now, here's the interesting part. As a bat closes in on an insect, it calls faster and faster. Researchers call this the feeding buzz. Why speed up? Well, more calls mean more updates, so the bat gets a sharper picture just when the insect is trying to escape.

M: And it's not a one-sided contest. Some moths have evolved ears that can detect bat calls. When they hear one, they suddenly drop or spiral toward the ground. A few tiger moths even produce clicks of their own, which can jam or confuse the bat's signal.
M: So you could think of this as an arms race. Every improvement on one side puts pressure on the other side to adapt.
M: Oh, and one common myth I want to clear up. Bats aren't blind. Most species can see perfectly well. Echolocation just works better in the dark, when vision isn't much help.

explanation: The professor says 'more calls mean more updates, so the bat gets a sharper picture.' More frequent information paraphrases 'more updates'. Moths drop toward the ground because they hear the calls, but the bat is not trying to scare them; nothing is said about weaker hearing.

text: Listen to part of a talk in a geology class.
script: W: Let's start with a question. How does solid rock end up hanging from a cave ceiling like an icicle? To answer that, we need to follow a single drop of water.

W: When rain falls, it picks up carbon dioxide from the air and, even more, from the soil. That makes the water slightly acidic. It's a weak acid, nothing dangerous, but it's strong enough to slowly dissolve limestone as it seeps down through cracks in the rock.

W: So the water now carries dissolved minerals. When it drips into an open cave, some of the carbon dioxide escapes into the cave air, and the water can't hold all of its mineral anymore. A tiny ring of calcite is left behind on the ceiling.

W: Drop after drop, that ring grows into a thin hollow tube. Cavers call these soda straws. If the tube gets blocked, water flows down the outside instead, and the formation thickens into a cone. That's a stalactite.
W: Meanwhile, water that falls to the floor builds a stalagmite upward. Given enough time, the two can meet and form a column.

W: And time is the key word here. Many of these formations grow less than a millimeter a year. That's why cave guides ask you not to touch them. Oil from your skin can stop the growth at that spot, and a broken one may take thousands of years to replace.

explanation: The professor says 'we need to follow a single drop of water' and then explains how soda straws, stalactites, stalagmites and columns form. She asks visitors not to touch formations, but she never says caves are dangerous; the weak acid is 'nothing dangerous'.

explanation: She says 'some of the carbon dioxide escapes into the cave air, and the water can't hold all of its mineral anymore.' Oil from skin is mentioned, but it stops growth rather than causing it, and freezing is never mentioned.

text: Listen to part of a talk in an astronomy class.
script: M: So, if you look at the Moon tonight and again next month, you'll see the same patterns, the same dark patches. Ever wondered why we never see the other side? The answer is something called tidal locking.

M: A lot of students assume this means the Moon doesn't spin. Actually, it does spin. It just turns once on its axis in exactly the time it takes to go around Earth once, about twenty-seven days. So the same face always points toward us.

M: How did that happen? Earth's gravity pulls a little harder on the near side of the Moon than on the far side, so the Moon gets stretched slightly into a bulge. Long ago the Moon spun faster, and Earth kept tugging on that bulge. Over millions of years, that tugging slowed the spin until it matched the orbit.

M: Now, you'll sometimes hear the far side called the dark side. That's misleading. It gets just as much sunlight as the side we see. It was only dark in the sense that it was unknown, at least until a spacecraft photographed it in nineteen fifty-nine.

M: And this isn't unique to our Moon. Pluto and its largest moon, Charon, are both locked, so each one always shows the same face to the other. In fact, the process is still going on here, too. Earth's own spin is very gradually slowing down.

explanation: He asks 'why we never see the other side?' and answers 'tidal locking,' then explains how it happened. The far side does not get less sunlight; he says it 'gets just as much sunlight as the side we see,' so that option reverses his point.

explanation: He says 'A lot of students assume this means the Moon doesn't spin. Actually, it does spin.' Not spinning means it has stopped rotating. The photograph from nineteen fifty-nine is about the far side, not about discovering tidal locking.

text: Listen to part of a talk in a psychology class.
script: W: Let's try a quick experiment in your heads. Imagine I read you a list of twenty words, just once, and then ask you to write down as many as you can. Which words do you think you'd remember?

W: If you're like most people, you'd remember the first few words and the last few words pretty well, and the ones in the middle would mostly disappear. Psychologists call this the serial position effect.

W: There are really two effects here. The advantage for the first items is called primacy. The idea is that when the list begins, you've got time to repeat those words to yourself, so they're more likely to get into long-term memory.
W: The advantage for the last items is called recency. Those words are still sitting in short-term memory when you start writing, so you can just, sort of, read them off.

W: Now, here's how we know these are separate processes. If you make people wait about thirty seconds before writing, and keep them busy, say, counting backward, the recency effect disappears. But the primacy effect stays. The delay wipes out short-term memory, but it doesn't touch what's already been stored.
W: And this has practical consequences. Think about a long day of job interviews. The candidates in the middle may be at a real disadvantage, through no fault of their own.

options: Ways to improve memory before an important exam
The differences between short-term memory in children and in adults

explanation: The professor describes 'the serial position effect': first and last words are remembered better than middle ones. The option about forgetting words heard once repeats the setup of the experiment, but the talk is about which words are remembered, depending on their position.

explanation: She introduces it with 'here's how we know these are separate processes': the delay removes recency but primacy stays. The method does not improve recall; it removes part of it, so the first option is wrong.

text: Listen to part of a talk in an anthropology class.
script: M: Think about the last graduation ceremony you went to. People wear unusual clothing, they walk across a stage one by one, and then suddenly they're graduates. Anthropologists have a name for events like this. They're called rites of passage.

M: The term comes from a French scholar, Arnold van Gennep, who wrote about it in the early nineteen hundreds. He noticed that ceremonies marking a change in status, like birth, adulthood or marriage, tended to share the same three-part structure, no matter which society he looked at.

M: First comes separation. The person is removed from their old role, sometimes physically, sometimes just symbolically, with a change of clothes, for example. Then there's a transition phase. And finally there's incorporation, when the person rejoins the community in their new role.

M: Now, the middle phase is the one later anthropologists found most fascinating. Victor Turner called it liminal, from the Latin word for threshold. During this phase, people are betwixt and between. They're no longer what they were, but not yet what they'll become. And often, everyone going through it together is treated as equal, whatever their background.
M: So, back to graduation. The gowns are identical for everyone, right? That's the liminal phase in action. Then you cross the stage, and you come out the other side with a new title.

options: To compare graduation ceremonies in different countries around the world
To explain a common structure found in many ceremonies
To argue that modern ceremonies have lost their meaning
To describe the life and career of Arnold van Gennep
explanation: The professor explains van Gennep's idea that ceremonies marking a change in status 'share the same three-part structure.' Graduation is used as one example, not compared across countries, and van Gennep is named only as the source of the term.

stem: According to the professor, what happens in the first phase of a rite of passage?

explanation: In separation, 'The person is removed from their old role.' Rejoining the community is the last phase, incorporation, and equal treatment belongs to the middle, liminal phase.

To illustrate the equality of the liminal phase
explanation: He says 'The gowns are identical for everyone' and adds 'That's the liminal phase in action,' linking back to people being 'treated as equal, whatever their background.' The word liminal comes from the Latin for threshold, not from the gowns.

explanation: He says the middle phase 'is the one later anthropologists found most fascinating' and then cites Victor Turner. Nothing is said about how long it lasts or about van Gennep thinking it unimportant.

text: Listen to part of a talk in an art history class.
script: W: Today we're looking at fresco, the technique behind many of the great wall paintings of Renaissance Italy, including Michelangelo's ceiling in the Sistine Chapel. The word fresco just means fresh in Italian, and that tells you a lot about how it works.

W: In true fresco, the artist paints onto wet lime plaster. The pigments are mixed only with water. There's no glue, no oil. So what holds the color on the wall? Well, as the plaster dries, it reacts with carbon dioxide in the air and forms a hard crystal layer, and the pigment gets locked inside it. The color becomes part of the wall itself.

W: But here's the catch. Plaster only stays wet for so many hours. So painters spread just enough fresh plaster for what they could finish in one day. These sections are called giornate, which means days. If you look closely at some frescoes, you can actually see the seams between one day's work and the next.
W: And mistakes? You can't just paint over them. The artist had to chip away the plaster and start that section again.

W: Some painters took a shortcut and painted on dry plaster instead. It's much more forgiving. The problem is that the paint just sits on the surface, so over the centuries a lot of it has flaked away, while true fresco has survived remarkably well.

explanation: The professor explains how pigment bonds with wet plaster and what that requires: working in daily sections and chipping away mistakes. Michelangelo's ceiling is only a famous example in the first line, so it is not the main topic.

text: Listen to part of a talk in a music class.
script: M: Here's a puzzle that bothered musicians for centuries. If you tune an instrument using perfectly pure intervals, the kind based on simple number ratios, it sounds beautiful in one key. But move to a distant key, and some chords sound terrible. Why?

M: Well, the math doesn't quite work out. Take the perfect fifth. If you stack twelve pure fifths on top of each other, you should end up on the same note, seven octaves higher. But you don't. You overshoot by a small amount. And that leftover has to go somewhere.

M: Older tuning systems hid the leftover in keys people rarely used. That worked fine, as long as composers stayed in the comfortable keys. Some intervals in the remote keys were so sour that musicians nicknamed one of them the wolf, because it howled.

M: The solution that eventually won is called equal temperament. You divide the octave into twelve exactly equal steps. That spreads the error evenly, so every interval except the octave is a tiny bit out of tune. Most listeners can't hear it, but every key is usable.
M: So it's a compromise. You give up a little purity, and in exchange you get total freedom to move between keys. By the late nineteenth century, it had become the standard way to tune pianos.

stem: What is the main topic of the talk?
options: How pianos are built so that they stay in tune for many years
Why composers avoided writing music in remote keys
The history of the perfect fifth in folk music
A tuning system that solved a mathematical problem
explanation: The professor explains that pure fifths do not add up evenly, 'the math doesn't quite work out,' and that equal temperament spreads the error. Remote keys are part of the problem he describes, but avoiding them is not the main topic.

stem: According to the professor, what happens when twelve pure fifths are stacked?
options: You land exactly seven octaves above the starting note
You go slightly past the note you expect
You produce an interval that musicians call the wolf because it sounds bad
You create the twelve steps of equal temperament
explanation: He says 'You overshoot by a small amount,' which means going slightly past the expected note. The first option is what 'should' happen, but he says 'But you don't,' so it reverses his point.

stem: Why does the professor mention the nickname 'the wolf'?
options: To show how bad some intervals sounded in older tunings
To explain where many musical terms come from
To give an example of an interval that is perfectly pure
To describe a well-known piece written long ago in a distant key
explanation: Some remote intervals were 'so sour' that one was called the wolf 'because it howled.' The nickname shows how out of tune they were. It is the opposite of a pure interval, so the third option reverses the meaning.

stem: What is the professor's view of equal temperament?
options: It is mathematically perfect and has no weaknesses
It makes music sound noticeably worse than older tunings did
It is a sensible trade-off between purity and flexibility
It became popular mainly because pianos are cheaper to build
explanation: He calls it 'a compromise': 'You give up a little purity' for 'total freedom to move between keys.' He also says 'Most listeners can't hear' the error, so it does not sound noticeably worse.

text: Listen to part of a talk in a business class.
script: W: In business, there's a popular belief that being first to market is the key to winning. It even has a name, first-mover advantage. Today I want to look at whether that belief really holds up.

W: There are some real benefits to going first. A first mover can build brand recognition before anyone else shows up. It can lock up scarce resources, like the best store locations or the most reliable suppliers. And sometimes it creates switching costs. Once customers have learned your system, moving to a competitor feels like a hassle.

W: But going first is also expensive. The pioneer has to convince people they need a product that's never existed before. It pays for all the trial and error. And here's the thing: competitors are watching. A second company, what we call a fast follower, can copy what worked, skip what didn't, and enter with a better product at a lower cost.
W: Think about internet search. The earliest search engines weren't the ones that ended up dominating. A later company studied what users wanted and simply did it better.
W: So my view is that timing matters, but being first isn't enough on its own. What matters more is whether a company can keep learning faster than the ones coming after it.

text: Listen to part of a talk in a linguistics class.
script: W: Imagine a busy port a few hundred years ago. Traders and workers arrive from many places, and they don't share a language. But they need to buy, sell, and work together. So what happens? Very often, a pidgin develops.

W: A pidgin is a simplified contact language. Most of its words usually come from the language of the most powerful group, but the grammar is stripped down. There may be no endings for tense or plural, and the word order is kept simple. And here's the important point. A pidgin is nobody's first language. Everyone who uses it speaks something else at home.

W: Now, things change when children are born into that community and grow up hearing the pidgin all around them. Those children don't just copy it. They expand it. Within a generation or two, it develops consistent ways to mark time, more complex sentences, and a much richer vocabulary. At that point, linguists call it a creole.

W: A good example is Tok Pisin, in Papua New Guinea. It started as a pidgin used on plantations. Today it has native speakers, it's used in newspapers and broadcasting, and it's one of the country's official languages.
W: So creoles show us something remarkable. Give children a limited system, and they'll build a full language out of it.

explanation: The professor explains how a pidgin forms and how, when children expand it, 'linguists call it a creole.' Papua New Guinea is only the setting of one example, Tok Pisin, so it is not the main topic.

text: Listen to part of a talk in an environmental science class.
script: M: Today's topic sounds like a good thing at first. More nutrients in a lake. Plants need nutrients, right? So how could extra food be a problem? Well, this process, called eutrophication, is one of the most common causes of poor water quality in the world.

M: It usually starts on land. Fertilizer from farms and lawns contains nitrogen and phosphorus. When it rains, some of that washes into streams and eventually into lakes or coastal waters. Untreated sewage can add even more.
M: Algae respond fast. They multiply into what we call a bloom, sometimes turning the water bright green. The bloom shades out the plants growing on the bottom, so those plants die.

M: But here's the twist. The real damage comes after the algae die. Bacteria break down all that dead material, and as they do, they use up the oxygen dissolved in the water. Fish and other animals that can't swim away suffocate. Areas like this are called dead zones. A large one forms in the Gulf of Mexico every summer, near the mouth of the Mississippi River.

M: The good news is that it can be reversed. In the nineteen seventies, several countries limited phosphates in laundry detergent, and some badly affected lakes recovered noticeably. Today, many farmers also plant strips of grass and trees along streams to catch fertilizer before it reaches the water.

explanation: The professor explains eutrophication: nitrogen and phosphorus wash into water, cause algal blooms, and lead to dead zones. Fertilizer is one source of nutrients, but the talk is not about how farmers choose amounts.

text: Listen to part of a talk in a biology class.
script: W: Last week we talked about warning coloration, how some poisonous or stinging animals advertise it with bright colors, so predators learn to leave them alone. Today, let's look at the cheaters.

W: In Batesian mimicry, a harmless species evolves to look like a dangerous one. Hoverflies are a nice example. They can't sting at all, but with their yellow and black stripes, a lot of birds, and a lot of people, mistake them for wasps.

W: Now, think about this from the predator's point of view. The trick only works because the predator has learned, maybe painfully, that the pattern means trouble. text: Listen to part of a talk in a psychology class.

text: Listen to part of a talk in an anthropology class.

text: Listen to part of a talk in a geology class.
script: M: Most volcanoes on Earth are found near the edges of tectonic plates, where plates pull apart or push together. But Hawaii is right in the middle of the Pacific Plate, thousands of kilometers from any edge. So why are there volcanoes there?

M: The leading explanation is called a hotspot. The idea, first proposed in the nineteen sixties, is that there's a fixed area of unusually hot material deep below the plate. It melts rock and feeds a volcano at the surface. Now, the key point is that the plate keeps moving, very slowly, toward the northwest, several centimeters a year. The hotspot stays put.

M: So what happens? A volcano forms over the hotspot, and then the plate carries it away. Cut off from its supply, it goes quiet, and a new volcano starts to form behind it. Over millions of years, you get a line of islands, like footprints.

M: And the evidence fits nicely. The Big Island, at the southeastern end, is the youngest, and it still has active volcanoes. As you move northwest, the islands get older, more eroded, and smaller. Kauai, near the other end, is about five million years old.

M: And here's a nice prediction. Off the southeast coast of the Big Island, there's an underwater volcano that's growing right now. Someday, probably tens of thousands of years from now, it'll break the surface and become the next Hawaiian island.

text: Listen to part of a talk in an astronomy class.
script: W: Here's a question I ask every year. Why is it hotter in summer than in winter? And every year, a lot of people say, because Earth is closer to the Sun in summer. It sounds reasonable. But it's wrong.

W: Here's a quick way to see why. Earth's orbit is almost a circle, but not quite, and we're actually closest to the Sun in early January. That's the middle of winter in the Northern Hemisphere. And another clue: when it's summer in Canada, it's winter in Argentina. If distance were the cause, both hemispheres would have summer at the same time.

W: So what's really going on? Earth's axis is tilted, by about twenty-three and a half degrees. As we travel around the Sun, that tilt stays pointed the same way in space. So for part of the year, the Northern Hemisphere leans toward the Sun, and for the other part, it leans away.

W: When your hemisphere leans toward the Sun, two things happen. First, sunlight hits the ground more directly. Think of a flashlight. Shine it straight down, and you get a small, bright spot. Tilt it, and the same light spreads over a bigger area, so each part gets less energy. Second, the days are longer, so there's more time to heat up.
W: So it's the angle, not the distance, that gives us our seasons.

To correct a common belief about the cause of seasons
To compare the climates of Canada and Argentina

explanation: She says many people think distance causes seasons, 'But it's wrong,' and ends with 'it's the angle, not the distance.' Canada, Argentina and the flashlight are only evidence and an analogy.

text: Listen to part of a talk in an educational psychology class.
script: M: Let's say you have ten hours to study for an exam. You could spend all ten hours the night before. Or you could spread them out, one hour a day over ten days. Same total time. Which works better?

M: Research going back more than a century gives a pretty clear answer. Spreading it out wins. This is called the spacing effect. One of the first people to document it was Hermann Ebbinghaus, a German psychologist in the eighteen eighties, who tested his own memory by learning long lists of nonsense syllables.

M: Now, here's what's tricky. Cramming often feels like it's working. Right after a long session, the material seems familiar, so you feel confident. And for a test the very next morning, cramming can do okay. The problem is what happens a week or a month later. Most of it is gone.

M: Why does spacing help? One popular explanation is that when you come back to material after a break, you've forgotten a little, so you have to work to pull it back up. And that effort seems to make the memory stronger.

M: In fact, many flashcard apps are built around this idea. They show you a card again just as you're about to forget it, and the gaps get longer each time. So, my advice: don't save it all for the night before. Your future self will thank you.

text: Listen to part of a talk in an anthropology class.
script: M: Today I want to talk about one of the most remarkable finds in the study of human origins. It's not a skull or a skeleton. It's a set of footprints.

M: In the late nineteen seventies, a team led by Mary Leakey was working at a site called Laetoli, in Tanzania. And they found a trail of footprints, preserved in hardened volcanic ash, about three point six million years old.

M: How could footprints possibly survive that long? Well, it took a lucky combination of events. A nearby volcano covered the area in a layer of fine ash. Then a light rain fell, turning the ash into something like wet cement. Animals walked across it, including at least two individuals who walked upright. The sun dried the ash hard, and then more ash buried it and protected it.

M: So what do the prints tell us? They show a heel striking the ground first, a raised arch, and a big toe lined up with the other toes, rather than sticking out to the side the way it does in a chimpanzee's foot. In other words, these individuals walked a lot like we do.

M: And here's why that matters. At that time, our ancestors still had small brains, not much bigger than a chimpanzee's. And the footprints are older than any stone tools we've found. So the footprints suggest that walking on two legs came first, long before big brains or toolmaking.

text: Listen to part of a talk in an art history class.
script: W: When we talk about Impressionism, we usually talk about the artists, Monet, Renoir, and their new way of seeing light. But today I want to talk about a much humbler object that helped make it possible: the paint tube.

W: Until the mid-eighteen hundreds, most painters, or their assistants, made paint by hand. They ground the colored powder and mixed it with oil in the studio. Storing it was a real problem. Paint was often kept in little bags made from animal bladders, which you'd poke with a tack to squeeze some out. They leaked, they burst, and the paint dried out quickly. So painting outdoors for a whole day just wasn't practical.

W: Then in eighteen forty-one, an American portrait painter living in London, John Rand, patented a small, squeezable metal tube that could be sealed with a cap. Suddenly, paint was portable and stayed fresh.

W: Now combine that with a few other changes, like folding easels and new railway lines out of the city, and painters could work directly in the countryside, catching changing light as it happened. Monet, for example, painted the same haystacks again and again at different times of day.

W: Renoir is often quoted as saying that without paint in tubes, there would have been no Impressionism. Maybe that's a slight exaggeration, but it makes a fair point. Sometimes a change in art depends on a change in technology.

text: Listen to part of a talk in a music theory class.
script: M: If you look at a page of music from the Baroque period, roughly sixteen hundred to seventeen fifty, you'll often notice something odd at the bottom. There's a bass line, and above or below some of the notes, there are little numbers. What are those numbers doing there?

M: They're part of a system called basso continuo, or just continuo. The word continuo means continuous, because this part plays all the way through the piece, underneath the melody. It was the foundation of almost all Baroque music.

M: The continuo was usually played by at least two people. One played the bass line on a low instrument, like a cello or a bassoon. The other played chords on a keyboard, like a harpsichord or an organ, or sometimes on a lute. But here's the interesting part. The composer didn't write out those chords. The keyboard player only got the bass line and those numbers, which showed which chords to play. The player had to make up the actual notes on the spot.
M: If that sounds familiar, it should. A jazz pianist reading chord symbols is doing something very similar. So Baroque keyboard players had to be skilled improvisers.

M: By the later seventeen hundreds, composers started writing out more of the parts in full, and the continuo slowly faded away. But for about a hundred and fifty years, you could hardly imagine music without it.

text: Listen to part of a talk in a linguistics class.
script: W: If you've ever listened to bilingual friends talking, you may have noticed them moving between two languages, sometimes in the middle of a single sentence. Linguists call this code-switching.

W: For a long time, people saw it as a sign of weakness. The assumption was that speakers switched because they didn't know either language well enough, so they grabbed whatever word came first. Some teachers even tried to discourage it.

W: But when researchers started recording real conversations, they found something very different. In a well-known study of Spanish and English speakers in New York around nineteen eighty, the speakers who switched most smoothly, even within sentences, tended to be the ones who were most fluent in both languages. And the switches weren't random. They tended to happen at points where the grammar of both languages fit together, so neither language's rules were broken.

W: So why do people switch? Often, it's social. A switch can show a shared identity, as if to say, we're part of the same community. It can add emphasis, or mark a quotation, when you repeat what someone said in the language they said it in. And sometimes, a word in one language just captures an idea better.
W: So rather than a sign of confusion, code-switching is now generally seen as a skill, a flexible use of two complete systems.

text: Listen to part of a talk in an environmental science class.
script: M: Most trees would die if you flooded their roots with seawater twice a day. But mangroves thrive in exactly those conditions, along tropical and subtropical coastlines around the world.

M: So how do they manage it? There are two big challenges: salt and oxygen. For salt, different species have different tricks. Some filter most of the salt out at the roots. Others take it in and then push it out through their leaves. You can sometimes see tiny salt crystals on the leaf surface.

M: Oxygen is the other problem. Coastal mud is waterlogged, so there's very little oxygen in it. Some mangroves solve this with roots that grow upward, sticking out of the mud like pencils. At low tide, these roots take in air.

M: Now, why should we care about mangroves? Well, that dense tangle of roots slows down waves and holds the soil in place, so mangroves protect the coastline from erosion and storm waves. The roots also make a sheltered nursery where young fish can grow up, away from larger predators. And mangrove soils store huge amounts of carbon, often more per hectare than many forests on land.

M: Unfortunately, large areas have been cleared over the past few decades, for shrimp farms and coastal building. The good news is that many countries are now replanting them, and when it's done in the right places, they can recover fairly well.
